outline.chapter_title: 1. Mathematical Reasoning in the Era of Large Language Models
outline.description: Introduces mathematical reasoning as a core challenge for language models, explains why open mathematical LLMs matter, and positions DeepSeekMath relative to closed and open models. This chapter frames the paper’s goals, main contributions, and the broader significance of building strong open-source math models.
subtopics: Why mathematical reasoning is difficult for language models
The gap between closed-source and open-source mathematical LLMs
What DeepSeekMath aims to achieve
Overview of DeepSeekMath-Base, DeepSeekMath-Instruct, and DeepSeekMath-RL
Two central ideas of the paper: large-scale math pre-training and reinforcement learning
Main benchmark headline results, including MATH and GSM8K
Why mathematical reasoning is a useful testbed for studying general reasoning

outline.chapter_title: 2. Foundations: Pre-Training, Instruction Tuning, and Reinforcement Learning for LLMs
outline.description: Builds the conceptual background needed to understand the paper. It reviews continual pre-training, instruction tuning, chain-of-thought prompting, program-aided reasoning, and policy optimization methods, giving students the tools to follow the later chapters.
subtopics: Continual pre-training and domain adaptation in language models
Instruction tuning and alignment
Chain-of-thought reasoning
Program-of-thought and tool-integrated reasoning
Few-shot vs zero-shot evaluation
Reward models and preference-based learning
Policy optimization basics: PPO and actor-critic methods
Why math is a special domain for training and evaluation

outline.chapter_title: 3. Building the DeepSeekMath Corpus from the Web
outline.description: Explains how the authors constructed a 120B-token mathematical corpus from Common Crawl. The chapter focuses on the data mining pipeline, iterative expansion strategy, domain discovery, human annotation, and contamination control.
subtopics: Why web-scale mathematical data is valuable
Using OpenWebMath as the initial seed corpus
Training a fastText classifier for math page retrieval
Positive and negative examples for classifier training
Deduplication and near-deduplication of Common Crawl
Ranking and selecting high-scoring math-related web pages
Iterative corpus expansion through domain-level analysis
Identifying math-related domains by collection density
Manual annotation of URL patterns within domains
Bootstrapping new positive examples for improved recall
Stopping criteria after multiple collection iterations
Benchmark decontamination using n-gram overlap filtering
Strengths and limitations of the data selection pipeline

outline.chapter_title: 4. Validating Corpus Quality: Why Data Matters More Than Size Alone
outline.description: Presents the empirical validation of the DeepSeekMath Corpus against existing math corpora. Students learn how corpus quality, multilinguality, and scale influence downstream mathematical reasoning.
subtopics: The role of corpus evaluation in domain-specific pre-training
Comparison corpora: MathPile, OpenWebMath, and Proof-Pile-2
Experimental setup with DeepSeek-LLM 1.3B
Training protocol for controlled corpus comparison
Evaluation benchmarks for English and Chinese math reasoning
Evidence that DeepSeekMath Corpus has higher average quality
Learning curve analysis and data scaling behavior
Multilingual coverage and its effect on Chinese benchmarks
Why small corpora plateau earlier during training
Interpreting corpus quality through downstream benchmark gains

outline.description: Describes the design and training of the base model, including initialization from a code model, the 500B-token training mixture, and the rationale behind combining math, code, arXiv, and natural language data.
subtopics: Why initialize from DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B
The hypothesis that code pre-training helps math reasoning
The 500B-token continual pre-training setup
Training data mixture: math, AlgebraicStack, arXiv, GitHub code, and natural language
Optimization settings and large-scale training choices
Balancing specialization with retention of general capabilities
Expected tradeoffs in domain adaptation

outline.chapter_title: 6. Evaluating the Base Model: Math, Tools, Formal Proofs, and General Reasoning
outline.description: Covers the comprehensive evaluation of DeepSeekMath-Base 7B. The chapter explains how the model performs across direct reasoning, program-aided solving, formal mathematics, and broader language, reasoning, and coding benchmarks.
subtopics: Evaluation philosophy for a mathematical base model
English and Chinese mathematical reasoning benchmarks
Few-shot chain-of-thought evaluation methodology
Performance on GSM8K, MATH, SAT, OCW, MMLU-STEM, MGSM-zh, CMATH, and Gaokao benchmarks
Why beating larger models like Minerva 540B is significant
Program-aided math evaluation with Python and symbolic libraries
Few-shot program-of-thought prompting
Results on GSM8K and MATH with tool use
Formal mathematics and informal-to-formal proving on miniF2F
Using Isabelle and Sledgehammer in proof autoformalization
General capability evaluation on MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, and MBPP
Evidence that math training improves general reasoning while preserving coding ability

outline.chapter_title: 7. Supervised Fine-Tuning for Mathematical Instruction Following
outline.description: Introduces the supervised fine-tuning stage that transforms the base model into an instruction-following math assistant. The chapter explains the curation of the 776K-example dataset and the move from raw capability to usable problem solving.
subtopics: Why supervised fine-tuning is needed after pre-training
Design goals for a mathematical instruction dataset
English data sources: GSM8K, MATH, MathInstruct, and Lila-OOD
Chinese data sources and K-12 topic coverage
Reasoning formats: chain-of-thought, program-of-thought, and tool-integrated reasoning
Balancing subject diversity and difficulty levels
Training setup for DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B
Concatenation and context-length management during SFT

outline.chapter_title: 8. Evaluating DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B Against Open and Closed Models
outline.description: Examines the instruction-tuned model’s performance in both no-tool and tool-augmented settings, comparing it with a wide range of open-source and proprietary systems.
subtopics: Why instruction-tuned evaluation differs from base-model evaluation
Benchmarking against GPT-4, Gemini, GLM-4, and other proprietary systems
Benchmarking against open-source general and math-specialized models
Step-by-step reasoning performance without tool use
Tool-integrated reasoning performance on quantitative math tasks
Strong MATH performance among open models
Comparison with much larger 70B-scale models
Remaining gap to top proprietary systems
What these results reveal about the value of targeted data and SFT

outline.chapter_title: 9. From PPO to GRPO: A More Efficient Reinforcement Learning Algorithm
outline.description: Develops the reinforcement learning core of the paper. This chapter explains standard PPO, its limitations for LLM math training, and the derivation and intuition of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
subtopics: Why reinforcement learning is applied after SFT
Review of PPO for language model alignment
The surrogate PPO objective and clipping mechanism
Advantage estimation and the role of the value function
KL regularization in PPO
Why critic training is costly for LLM-scale RL
The challenge of sparse end-of-sequence rewards in math tasks
The key idea of GRPO: group-relative baselines
Sampling multiple outputs per prompt
Using group mean and variance to compute relative advantages
The GRPO objective function
Direct KL regularization in the loss rather than the reward
The unbiased KL divergence estimator used in GRPO
Memory and efficiency advantages of removing the critic

outline.chapter_title: 10. Outcome Supervision, Process Supervision, and Iterative RL
outline.description: Expands the GRPO framework into practical variants and training strategies. Students learn the difference between rewarding final answers and intermediate reasoning steps, as well as why reward models must evolve during training.
subtopics: Outcome supervision in RL for mathematical reasoning
Normalized final-sequence rewards as token-level advantages
Process supervision and step-level reward signals
Computing advantages from future step rewards
When process supervision is more informative than outcome supervision
Iterative RL with alternating policy and reward model updates
Replay mechanisms for reward model stability
Algorithmic workflow of iterative GRPO
Tradeoffs among simplicity, signal quality, and compute cost

outline.description: Presents the reinforcement learning experiments built on DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B. The chapter details the RL training setup, reward model construction, evaluation protocol, and the final gains achieved by GRPO.
subtopics: RL training data drawn from GSM8K and MATH chain-of-thought questions
Why the RL stage uses only a subset of the SFT data
Reward model training based on DeepSeekMath-Base 7B
GRPO hyperparameters: learning rate, KL coefficient, group size, and batch size
Single update after each exploration stage
Defining in-domain and out-of-domain evaluation tasks
Performance gains on GSM8K and MATH
Improvements on Chinese and other out-of-domain benchmarks
Why the RL improvements are notable despite narrow RL training data
Self-consistency and multi-sample decoding results

outline.chapter_title: 12. Pre-Training Lessons: Code Helps, arXiv Does Not Always
outline.description: Synthesizes the paper’s major ablation findings about data composition. This chapter focuses on what kinds of pre-training data actually improve mathematical reasoning and why some common assumptions do not hold.
subtopics: The hypothesis that code training improves reasoning
Two-stage training: code then math vs general then math
One-stage training: math only vs mixed code and math
Effects on tool-free mathematical reasoning
Effects on program-aided mathematical reasoning
Catastrophic forgetting and how mixed training can mitigate it
Interaction between model size and multi-domain learning
The widespread use of arXiv in math pre-training
Experiments with MathPile and ArXiv-RedPajama
Why arXiv-only training showed little or negative benefit in this study
Caveats and limits of the arXiv conclusion
What these findings imply for future domain-specific corpus design

outline.chapter_title: 13. A Unified View of SFT, RFT, DPO, PPO, and GRPO
outline.description: Reframes multiple alignment and post-training methods under a shared mathematical perspective. This chapter teaches students how to compare diverse methods in terms of data source, reward function, and gradient coefficient.
subtopics: Motivation for a unified paradigm
The generic gradient form across post-training methods
Key components: data source, reward function, and algorithm
Supervised Fine-Tuning as a special case
Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT)
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
Online RFT
PPO and GRPO within the same framework
Offline sampling vs online sampling
Rule-based rewards vs learned reward models
Why online training can outperform offline methods
Why graded positive and negative reinforcement matters
How process supervision changes the gradient signal

outline.chapter_title: 14. Why Reinforcement Learning Works Here—and What It Does Not Yet Solve
outline.description: Analyzes the mechanism behind the observed RL gains. Rather than treating RL improvements as mysterious, this chapter explains them in terms of output distribution shaping, majority-vote robustness, and limits on fundamental capability gains.
subtopics: Pass@K vs Maj@K as diagnostic tools
Evidence that RL improves Maj@K more than Pass@K
Distribution shaping vs true capability expansion
The notion of misalignment in reasoning models after SFT
How RL may elevate correct outputs already present in the model
Implications for interpreting benchmark gains
What this means for the design of future RL pipelines

outline.chapter_title: 15. Future Directions for More Effective Reinforcement Learning
outline.description: Explores the paper’s forward-looking ideas for improving RL in language models, using the unified paradigm to organize research directions around data, algorithms, and reward functions.
subtopics: Improving the data source with out-of-distribution prompts
Advanced sampling and search-based decoding during exploration
Efficient inference methods for better RL exploration
Robust algorithms under noisy reward signals
Weak-to-strong alignment ideas
Improving reward model generalization
Modeling reward uncertainty
Building better process reward models at scale
How future RL might move from distribution stabilization to capability gains

outline.chapter_title: 16. Limitations, Broader Lessons, and the Open Math LLM Roadmap
outline.description: Concludes the textbook by summarizing the paper’s achievements, practical limitations, and broader lessons for building specialized open language models. It also reflects on where DeepSeekMath is still weaker and what comes next.
subtopics: Summary of DeepSeekMath’s main achievements
Why a 7B open model can approach far larger or proprietary systems
Current weaknesses in geometry and theorem proving
Few-shot limitations relative to GPT-4
Possible data selection biases in pre-training and fine-tuning
The broader lesson that high-quality domain data can rival sheer parameter scale
The role of code pre-training in reasoning-oriented models
Open problems in mathematical reasoning for LLMs
Future work in corpus construction, reward modeling, and RL design
